original_question: Fix any graph G with three vertices and any k >= 2. Assuming over RCA0 the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of triples of natural numbers, does it follow that every coloring of copies of G in the Rado graph into countably many colors, with each color used at most k times, has a subgraph isomorphic to the Rado graph in which no two copies of G receive the same color?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Open problem (3): "What about k-bounded colorings of graphs with three vertices in the Rado graph versus k-bounded colorings of triples of natural numbers? That is, assuming the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of triples of natural numbers, does the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of copies of G in the Rado graph follow over RCA0, where G is any graph on three vertices?"
correct_elements: Your draft already targets the correct open problem, keeps the scope to graphs G with exactly three vertices, uses the correct base theory RCA0, correctly frames the implication from the rainbow Ramsey theorem for triples of natural numbers to the rainbow Ramsey theorem for copies of G in the Rado graph, and correctly spells out the intended rainbow conclusion inside a subgraph isomorphic to the Rado graph. It also correctly includes the k-boundedness condition and the use of countably many colors.
missing_details: The antecedent should be made fully explicit as the rainbow Ramsey theorem for 3-element subsets of N: every coloring f:[N]^3 -> N such that each color is used at most k times has an infinite set H subseteq N on which f is injective.

The consequent should be stated explicitly as a principle about the countable Rado graph R: every coloring c of all copies of G in R into N such that each color is used at most k times has a subgraph R' subseteq R with R' isomorphic to R on which c is injective on the copies of G.
The universal quantifiers should be stated explicitly: the question is for every graph G on exactly three vertices and every integer k >= 2.
For full stand-alone clarity, the ambient structure should be named as the countable Rado graph R.
The phrase 'triples of natural numbers' should be formalized as 3-element subsets of N, since that is the standard reverse-mathematical formulation.
refined_question: For each graph G on exactly three vertices and each integer k >= 2, does RCA0 prove the following implication: if every k-bounded coloring f:[N]^3 -> N admits an infinite set H subseteq N such that f is injective on [H]^3, then every k-bounded coloring c of all copies of G in the countable Rado graph R into N admits a subgraph R' subseteq R with R' isomorphic to R such that c is injective on the copies of G contained in R'?
justification: The draft is essentially a paraphrase of Section 2, Open problem (3). The surrounding motivation defines exactly what the paper means by the rainbow Ramsey property for the Rado graph: for any finite graph G and k >= 2, any coloring of the copies of G in R into omega many colors with each color used at most k times has a subgraph R' of R, again a Rado graph, in which no two copies of G have the same color. Statement (D) then packages this property for each k >= 2. The only real gap in the draft is that the antecedent principle on triples of natural numbers is not formalized as a sentence over RCA0, and the quantifiers over G and k should be made completely explicit. No paper-stated equivalent reformulation of Open problem (3) is given.
